person_title: Chief Executive Officer of Nimbus Cascade Robotics
item_title: Building warehouse robots that learn on the floor
transcript_text:
[Priya Chandrasekaran] Maren, thanks for making the time. Let's start with the basics -- what does Nimbus Cascade actually build?
[Maren Okafor] Happy to be here. We build the picking arms and the routing software that sits on top of them for mid-size distribution centers -- the kind of warehouse that's too small to justify a fully custom automation line but still ships tens of thousands of orders a day. Our arms use a shared perception model across every site we deploy, so a mistake one robot makes in Ohio becomes a lesson every other robot in the fleet gets by the next nightly update.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] That fleet-learning idea is central to your pitch. How does it actually work day to day?
[Maren Okafor] Every arm logs the grasps it attempts and whether the item made it into the tote cleanly. Those logs get pooled centrally, and we retrain the grasp-selection model on the combined set every night. So a new plastic-wrapped item that trips up an arm in Reno on Monday is something every other arm in the network has already learned to handle by Tuesday morning, even in a facility that's never seen that item before. The individual robot is dumb by design -- the fleet is where the intelligence lives.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] Doesn't that centralization worry your customers, given how sensitive warehouse operations data can be?
[Maren Okafor] It comes up in almost every sales conversation. What we pool is grasp geometry and outcome -- did the gripper close correctly, did the item drop -- not order contents, not customer information, not anything that would tell you what the warehouse actually ships. We drew that line early because we knew it would be a sticking point, and honestly it's made the sales conversations easier, not harder, once people see the actual data schema.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] You started as a computer vision researcher before founding the company. What made you jump into hardware?
[Maren Okafor] I spent four years publishing papers on object recognition and slowly realized the hard part was never the model anymore -- it was the last six inches between a camera's prediction and a gripper actually closing around an oddly shaped object without crushing it or dropping it. Software people kept treating that as someone else's problem. I got tired of it being nobody's problem, so I started a company where it had to be mine.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] What's the single biggest technical obstacle left in this space?
[Maren Okafor] Deformable packaging, without question. A rigid box is a solved problem at this point -- any competent vision system can handle it. A bag of shredded packing material, a soft mailer, a loose garment bag -- those still fool our models more often than I'd like to admit. We've cut our error rate on deformables by more than half in the last year, but it's the long tail we spend most of our engineering time on now.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] How big is the team today, and where's headcount growing?
[Maren Okafor] We're just under two hundred people. The fastest-growing group isn't engineering anymore, somewhat to my surprise -- it's field deployment. Every new site needs someone on the ground for the first six weeks tuning the perception model to that specific facility's lighting and shelving, and we underestimated how much that mattered when we were smaller.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] Where do you see the company in five years?
[Maren Okafor] Honestly, boring. I want warehouse robotics to be as unremarkable as a conveyor belt -- something a facility manager orders because it's the obvious choice, not because it's a bet on a startup. When nobody writes articles about us anymore because robotic picking is just how warehouses work, that's when I'll know we did our job.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] Last question -- what keeps you up at night right now?
[Maren Okafor] Supply chain risk on the actuator components, honestly, more than any AI problem. We're a hardware company that happens to have a very good software story, and people forget the hardware constraints don't go away just because the model gets smarter. A six-week lead time slip on a motor controller can hurt us more than any algorithm regression.
[Priya Chandrasekaran] Maren, thank you for walking through all of that.
[Maren Okafor] Thanks for having me -- this was fun.

person_title: Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer of Fernglass Analytics
item_title: Why every data platform is suddenly a query-cost story
transcript_text:
[Rosa Fitzgerald] Devon, Fernglass has been pretty vocal that the analytics market is about to go through a repricing. Walk me through what you mean.
[Devon Holt] For a decade, the pitch in this industry was store everything, query it however you want, worry about cost later. That worked when compute was getting cheaper every year faster than data volumes were growing. Those curves crossed about two years ago for most of our customers -- data volume is now growing faster than the hardware is getting cheaper, and companies are getting bills that finally make them ask what they're actually querying and why.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] So what does Fernglass do differently?
[Devon Holt] We push a lot of the aggregation work down to write time instead of query time. If you know ninety percent of your dashboards ask for daily rollups by region, you shouldn't be scanning raw event tables every single time someone opens that dashboard. It sounds almost too simple to be a company, but getting the rollup logic right without silently going stale is most of the engineering.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] Isn't that just a caching layer with a different name?
[Devon Holt] People say that a lot, and I understand why, but a cache assumes the underlying query is still the source of truth and you're just avoiding recomputation. We're closer to a second, purpose-built representation of the data that we keep continuously consistent with the source. The distinction matters operationally -- a stale cache just means a slow refresh, a wrong rollup means someone makes a decision off bad numbers, so we test it completely differently.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] You came out of a big cloud data warehouse before founding Fernglass. What did that job teach you that you couldn't unlearn?
[Devon Holt] That most customers don't actually want more power, they want a smaller bill and the same three dashboards to keep working. We spent years building increasingly exotic query capabilities that maybe five percent of accounts ever touched, while the other ninety-five percent just wanted their existing reports to run faster and cheaper. Fernglass exists because I got tired of building for the five percent.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] How do you think about competing against the incumbents who could, in theory, just build this themselves?
[Devon Holt] They could, and a couple of them are trying. But it's a genuinely awkward feature for an incumbent to ship, because it's an admission that their default behavior was wasteful. We don't have that conflict -- being cheap and fast is the entire premise of the company, not a defensive add-on bolted onto a larger platform.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] What's a prediction you'd make about this market that most people would push back on?
[Devon Holt] That raw storage cost stops mattering as a marketing point within three years, and query efficiency becomes the only number anyone quotes. Storage is already commodity-cheap. The differentiator is entirely going to be how little compute you burn extracting an answer from that storage, and most of the industry is still marketing itself around the wrong number.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] Any regrets about how you built the company so far?
[Devon Holt] We spent our first year building for enterprise contracts we didn't have yet, adding configurability nobody asked for. It took a blunt conversation with an early customer -- who told us she just wanted the default settings to be good -- to get us to rip half of it back out. Configurability is a tax on every future engineer who touches the code, and we paid that tax for a year before we needed to.
[Rosa Fitzgerald] Devon, this has been great. Thanks for coming on.
[Devon Holt] Thanks, Rosa. Always enjoy these.

person_title: Chief Medical Officer of Solace Peak Health
item_title: Inside the launch of Solace Peak's triage assistant
transcript_text:
[Marcus Ubaldi] Dr. Nandakumar, congratulations on the launch this week. For listeners who haven't seen the announcement, what did Solace Peak actually ship?
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] Thank you, Marcus. We shipped Corvus, our triage assistant for urgent care intake. It listens to the intake conversation with the patient's consent, drafts a structured summary for the clinician, and flags a small set of symptom combinations that historically get under-triaged in a busy waiting room -- things like atypical chest pain presentations in younger patients.
[Marcus Ubaldi] How long was this in development before today?
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] A little over two years from first prototype to this launch, and honestly most of that time went into the parts nobody sees in a demo -- the audit trail, the clinician override workflow, getting our false-flag rate down to something a busy intake nurse could actually tolerate without alarm fatigue setting in within a week.
[Marcus Ubaldi] Alarm fatigue is a real concern in this field. How did you actually address it rather than just claim you had?
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] We ran an eighteen-month pilot across four partner clinics where Corvus's flags were logged but not shown to staff, purely to measure precision against what those clinics' own retrospective chart review found. We didn't turn the flags on for clinicians until the false-positive rate on that unseen data was under one in twenty. That threshold was non-negotiable for me, even when it meant delaying launch twice.
[Marcus Ubaldi] Delaying launch twice couldn't have been an easy sell internally.
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] It wasn't, and I'll be honest that there was real pressure from the business side both times. But I've worked the floor of an urgent care clinic, and a tool that cries wolf gets ignored within a month, at which point it's worse than useless -- it's actively dangerous because staff stop trusting the entire system, including the parts that are right. I'd rather ship late and trusted than early and ignored.
[Marcus Ubaldi] What was the hardest engineering problem, separate from the clinical validation?
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] Getting the transcription accurate enough in a genuinely loud waiting room environment, with multiple conversations overlapping and children crying in the background. Our error rate in a quiet consult room versus a Friday evening urgent care lobby was night and day for the first year, and closing that gap took more audio engineering work than the actual triage logic did.
[Marcus Ubaldi] What happens next -- what's the roadmap beyond today's launch?
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] Next is pediatric intake specifically, which has its own vocabulary and presentation patterns that our current model wasn't trained deeply enough on. After that, we want to extend the same flagging logic to telehealth intake calls, where the audio problem is different but arguably just as hard.
[Marcus Ubaldi] Any final message for clinicians who are skeptical of tools like this?
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] Be skeptical -- please. Ask us for our false-positive and false-negative rates on your own patient population before you trust a single flag, and if a vendor won't give you those numbers, that tells you something. We built Corvus to be interrogated, not just adopted.
[Marcus Ubaldi] Dr. Nandakumar, thank you so much for the time today.
[Dr. Priya Nandakumar] Thank you for having me, Marcus.

person_title: Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Ferrovia Motors
item_title: Ferrovia unveils the Meridian utility van
transcript_text:
[Nadia Ferris] Elias, the Meridian is finally out from behind the curtain. Why a delivery van, of all the vehicles Ferrovia could have started with?
[Elias Thornbury] Because vans are boring, and boring is where the economics actually work. Nobody buys a delivery van for the styling -- fleet operators buy on total cost per mile, and that's a spreadsheet argument we can win today with the battery chemistry we have, unlike a lot of the flashier categories the industry likes to launch with first.
[Nadia Ferris] Walk us through the numbers you're claiming on cost per mile.
[Elias Thornbury] We're quoting eleven cents a mile in energy and scheduled maintenance combined for a fleet operator running the Meridian on a typical urban route, against roughly twenty-six cents for a comparable diesel van once you include fuel, oil changes, and the brake wear that regenerative braking mostly eliminates. That gap is what gets a fleet manager to sign, not the acceleration numbers.
[Nadia Ferris] Range has been the sticking point for commercial EVs in this category. What are you delivering?
[Elias Thornbury] Two hundred and ten miles loaded, which covers the overwhelming majority of urban and regional delivery routes with margin to spare. We made a deliberate choice not to chase a bigger number by adding battery weight, because every extra pound of battery is a pound of cargo the operator can't carry, and cargo capacity is what they're actually buying a van for.
[Nadia Ferris] You came from an aerospace background before this. How much of that shows up in the Meridian?
[Elias Thornbury] More than people expect. The battery enclosure design borrows directly from techniques we used for equipment housings that had to survive vibration and thermal cycling for a decade without maintenance. A delivery van's duty cycle -- stop and go, all day, every day, for years -- is a much closer cousin to that world than to a passenger car's.
[Nadia Ferris] When do the first units actually reach customers?
[Elias Thornbury] Fleet pilots start in the fourth quarter with three regional logistics partners we've been testing prototypes with for the better part of a year. Broader production deliveries follow in the first half of next year, once we've worked through whatever those pilots surface that our own testing didn't catch.
[Nadia Ferris] What's the biggest risk to that timeline, in your own assessment?
[Elias Thornbury] Battery cell supply, without question. We've dual-sourced our cells specifically to protect against this, but the whole industry is still bidding for the same limited pool of manufacturing capacity, and I'd be lying if I said a supply shock couldn't push our production ramp by a quarter or two.
[Nadia Ferris] How are you thinking about competition from the established truck manufacturers entering this space?
[Elias Thornbury] They have manufacturing scale we don't have yet, and I take that seriously. What we have is a vehicle designed as an EV from the frame up rather than an existing diesel platform with a battery bolted in, and that shows up in weight distribution and cargo volume in ways a retrofit design can't easily match.
[Nadia Ferris] Elias, congratulations again on the reveal, and thanks for walking us through it.
[Elias Thornbury] Thanks, Nadia. Glad to finally have it out in the open after two years of secrecy.

person_title: Chief Executive Officer of Kelpwave Ocean Data
item_title: The market finally wants to pay for ocean sensor data
transcript_text:
[Tobias Reyment] Ingrid, Kelpwave has been quietly profitable for two years in a sector most people assume runs on grant money. How?
[Ingrid Solberg] We stopped thinking of ourselves as a research project a long time ago and started thinking of ourselves as an insurance data vendor that happens to use buoys. Shipping insurers, offshore wind operators, and fisheries all need the same underlying ocean temperature and current data, just packaged differently, and they have real budgets for exactly that.
[Tobias Reyment] What changed in the market to make that viable now, versus five years ago?
[Ingrid Solberg] Offshore wind, mostly. Every new wind farm has to model wave loading and current patterns for decades of expected operation before it's financeable, and that modeling is only as good as the historical sensor data underneath it. Five years ago that data barely existed at the resolution insurers wanted. We built the network that fills that gap, and the timing happened to line up with the wind buildout.
[Tobias Reyment] How many buoys are actually in the water right now?
[Ingrid Solberg] A little over four hundred across three ocean basins, each one relaying temperature, salinity, and current data back over satellite link every fifteen minutes. We're adding roughly thirty a quarter right now, mostly to densify coverage in areas where wind development is accelerating fastest.
[Tobias Reyment] What's the actual failure mode for a buoy out there? What breaks first?
[Ingrid Solberg] Biofouling, overwhelmingly. Barnacles and algae growth on the sensor housing degrade reading accuracy long before any electronics actually fail. We've gone through four generations of anti-fouling coating, and it's still the single line item that determines how often we have to physically service a unit.
[Tobias Reyment] You have a research background yourself. Was there a specific moment you decided to commercialize this instead of staying in academia?
[Ingrid Solberg] I spent a field season watching a fishery collapse partly because nobody had current data granular enough to explain a spawning ground shift until it was too late to act on. That was the moment I realized the data existing in a published paper two years after the fact helps nobody who actually needed to act on it in real time. Commercial customers pay for real time. Journals don't.
[Tobias Reyment] Where do you see the biggest growth opportunity over the next few years?
[Ingrid Solberg] Reinsurance, honestly. As climate-linked claims on coastal and offshore assets keep climbing, the reinsurers underwriting those policies want independent, high-resolution environmental data they don't have to take a single insurer's word for. That's a market with real budgets and a growing, structural need.
[Tobias Reyment] Any part of the business that still feels fragile to you?
[Ingrid Solberg] The satellite relay costs. We're at the mercy of a small number of providers for the uplink, and if those prices moved sharply it would hit our margins faster than almost anything else in the business. We're exploring a mesh relay approach between buoys to reduce that dependency, but it's still early.
[Tobias Reyment] Ingrid, thank you for the conversation.
[Ingrid Solberg] Thanks for having me, Tobias -- always glad to talk about the unglamorous parts of this business.

person_title: Creative Director and Chief Executive Officer of Cobalt Loom Studios
item_title: Running a game studio without crunch, five years in
transcript_text:
[Halle Duquette] Marcus, Cobalt Loom has built a reputation as one of the few mid-size studios that genuinely doesn't crunch before launch. How do you actually make that hold up under deadline pressure?
[Marcus Reyes] The honest answer is we ship less scope, not that we're more efficient than everyone else. Every studio that crunches is usually crunching because the scope was fixed and the schedule was fixed, so the only variable left to burn is people's hours. We treat scope as the variable instead, and we cut features, not people's evenings, when a milestone is at risk.
[Halle Duquette] That sounds simple in theory. What does it look like in an actual crunch-adjacent moment?
[Marcus Reyes] Six weeks before our last launch, our co-op mode wasn't going to be stable in time. The old instinct in this industry is to push the team to nights and weekends to save it. Instead we cut co-op from the launch build entirely and shipped it as a free update two months later, fully tested, with the team that built it rested enough to actually do good work on the patch.
[Halle Duquette] How did the team react to cutting a feature that close to launch?
[Marcus Reyes] There was real disappointment, I won't pretend otherwise -- people had put months into that mode. But I've watched enough crunched launches ship broken, buggy features that get torn apart in reviews, and a delayed, working feature beats a rushed, broken one every time. Once people saw the post-launch update land clean, the frustration mostly turned into relief.
[Halle Duquette] You came up as an artist, not a producer or an executive. How has that shaped how you run the studio?
[Marcus Reyes] I still remember exactly what it felt like to be handed an impossible deadline by someone who'd never had to sit at the desk and do the actual work themselves. I try never to schedule a milestone I haven't personally sat with an artist or engineer to sanity-check first. It slows down planning, but it means I'm not asking for things I don't actually understand the cost of.
[Halle Duquette] What's the trade-off nobody warns you about when you commit to a no-crunch culture?
[Marcus Reyes] Slower iteration on ambitious mechanics, honestly. Some of the most interesting ideas in games only get discovered through a lot of rapid, exhausting prototyping, and a healthier pace means fewer of those late-night discovery sessions. We've had to get more deliberate about prototyping earlier in the schedule to compensate, rather than relying on a crunch period to find the magic.
[Halle Duquette] How do you keep that culture intact as the studio grows? You're triple the headcount you were at founding.
[Marcus Reyes] Every new lead we hire goes through a conversation, before they're offered the role, about a real scope cut we made and why. If someone's instinct in that conversation is that we should have just pushed the team instead, that's usually a sign the culture fit isn't there, no matter how talented they are.
[Halle Duquette] Any regrets from the studio's first few years that you'd handle differently now?
[Marcus Reyes] Our very first title did have a rough patch of crunch near the end, before we'd formalized any of this. I think about that project's launch a lot, and it's honestly the reason the rest of these policies exist. We built the culture out of a mistake, not out of some plan we had from day one.
[Halle Duquette] Marcus, this was great. Thanks so much for coming on.
[Marcus Reyes] Thank you, Halle. Good questions, as always.

item_title: What a vertical farming startup learned from its own failures
transcript_text:
[Owen Baptiste] Aisha, Verdant Row had a pretty public crop failure two years ago that a lot of outlets covered. How did that shape the company culture that exists today?
[Aisha Bello] It's honestly the single event I'd point to if you asked what culture actually means here now. We lost about sixty percent of a lettuce cycle to a nutrient dosing error, and the engineer who made the configuration mistake came to me directly instead of trying to quietly patch it. That decision, more than any values poster on a wall, is what set the tone for everything after.
[Owen Baptiste] What did you do in that moment that you think mattered?
[Aisha Bello] I made sure the postmortem we ran was about the system, not about her. We'd shipped a dosing interface that let you enter a value without any sanity-check range, and that was our failure as much as the mis-entered number was hers. If we'd punished the person instead of fixing the interface, the next person to make a similar mistake would have hidden it instead of reporting it, and that's a much worse outcome for a farm running on tight margins.
[Owen Baptiste] How do you hire for that kind of transparency? It's easy to say you want it, harder to actually select for it.
[Aisha Bello] We ask every candidate to describe a mistake they made at a previous job and what happened afterward, not just what the mistake was. The answer that worries me isn't a bad mistake -- everyone has one -- it's someone who can only describe mistakes that were caught by someone else rather than ones they surfaced themselves.
[Owen Baptiste] Vertical farming as an industry has had a rough couple of years financially. How has that affected morale internally?
[Aisha Bello] We've had to be honest with the team about which of our competitors' failures are industry-wide problems and which were self-inflicted, because the instinct when you read bad industry news every week is to assume your own company is next. Most of the shutdowns we've watched came from overbuilding physical capacity before the unit economics were proven, which is specifically the mistake we've refused to make, even when investors pushed us to grow the footprint faster.
[Owen Baptiste] Was there real pressure to grow the physical footprint faster than you wanted to?
[Aisha Bello] Constant pressure, yes, especially in the year after our first funding round closed. I said no to a facility expansion that would have doubled our square footage before we'd gotten yield-per-square-foot on our existing facility to where I wanted it. That was an uncomfortable board conversation, but I think it's the single decision that kept us solvent while three competitors that made the opposite choice didn't survive.
[Owen Baptiste] What does the culture look like day to day on the farm floor versus in a typical office job?
[Aisha Bello] Everyone, including me, still does a rotation on the floor monthly -- harvesting, cleaning racks, calibrating sensors. It's partly practical, since floor staff catch equipment issues before they become expensive, but it's also a leveling mechanism. It's hard to make an out-of-touch decision about floor operations when you were physically on that floor three weeks ago.
[Owen Baptiste] Aisha, thank you for such an honest conversation.
[Aisha Bello] Thank you, Owen. I'd rather talk about the failure than pretend it didn't happen.

person_title: Chief Executive Officer of Halcyon Ledger
item_title: Cross-border settlement is quietly getting rebuilt
transcript_text:
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] Tomas, Halcyon Ledger describes itself as plumbing, not a product. What's the distinction you're drawing there?
[Tomas Vrba] A product is something a customer chooses because they like it. Plumbing is something they never think about as long as it works, and get furious about the moment it doesn't. We build the settlement layer that banks route cross-border payments through overnight, and our entire job is to be invisible. If a merchant or a customer ever has to think about Halcyon by name, something has already gone wrong.
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] Cross-border settlement has traditionally been slow because of correspondent banking chains. How does your approach actually shorten that?
[Tomas Vrba] We net obligations between participating banks in near real time instead of settling every transaction individually through a chain of intermediaries, each adding its own delay and fee. A hundred small payments between the same two banks over a day become one net settlement at the end of the window. That netting is the whole trick -- it's not new mathematically, it's just newly practical at the volume and speed our infrastructure runs at.
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] What made this practical now that wasn't practical a decade ago?
[Tomas Vrba] Regulatory appetite, more than technology, if I'm honest. The computational side of real-time netting has been solvable for years. What changed is that enough central banks have gotten comfortable enough with real-time gross settlement infrastructure that a private netting layer on top of it is no longer treated as a novelty risk in a regulatory review -- it's treated as a known category now.
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] How many banks are actually routing volume through Halcyon today?
[Tomas Vrba] Thirty-one banks across nine currency corridors, with three more corridors in active regulatory review right now. Growth is corridor by corridor rather than bank by bank, since each new currency pair requires its own separate approval process with the relevant central banks on both sides.
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] What's the scariest failure mode for a company doing what you do?
[Tomas Vrba] A netting error that goes undetected for even a few hours during a high-volume window. We've built in redundant reconciliation checks specifically because the cost of a mistake here isn't a bad user experience, it's actual money moving to the wrong place at scale, and unwinding that after the fact between multiple banks and multiple jurisdictions is its own nightmare.
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] How do you think about competition from central bank digital currency projects that could, in principle, do some of this themselves?
[Tomas Vrba] We see those as more likely to be a foundation we settle on top of than a competitor. A central bank digital currency solves the trust and finality problem for the underlying currency, but the netting and routing layer across corridors is still a distinct problem, and it's the one we're built for. I'd rather compete by being the best netting layer than compete with a central bank on issuing currency.
[Greta Lindqvist-Amoah] Tomas, thank you for the time and the clarity.
[Tomas Vrba] Thank you, Greta. Glad to make the boring parts of finance a little less mysterious.

person_title: Chief Scientist at Pinewood Cognitive Systems
item_title: Why Pinewood is betting on smaller, narrower models
transcript_text:
[Femi Aduba] Dr. Lindqvist, Pinewood has taken a fairly contrarian stance in the current environment, focusing on small, specialized models instead of chasing scale. Why?
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] Because most of our customers don't need a model that can write poetry and also do calculus and also hold a philosophical debate. They need a model that reliably extracts line items from a specific kind of invoice, or classifies a specific kind of support ticket, at a cost and latency that a general-purpose frontier model simply isn't built to hit. We think the market has room for both approaches, and we deliberately picked the less crowded one.
[Femi Aduba] What's the actual technical advantage of narrow specialization, beyond just cost?
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] Predictability, which matters enormously in regulated or high-stakes settings. A narrow model trained on a well-defined task has a failure distribution you can actually characterize and test against. A general-purpose model's failure modes are much harder to fully enumerate, because the space of things it might be asked to do is nearly unbounded. Our customers in insurance and logistics care about that predictability more than raw capability.
[Femi Aduba] Doesn't that leave you exposed if general models keep getting cheaper and just absorb your niche?
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] It's the risk we think about most, honestly. Our answer is that even if a general model becomes cheap enough to run for our use cases, a customer in a regulated industry still needs a model whose behavior on their specific task has been independently validated and documented, and that validation layer is a real and durable part of what we sell, separate from the raw model weights themselves.
[Femi Aduba] How big are the models you're actually shipping, roughly?
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] Small enough to run on a single commodity GPU per model, in most cases, which matters a lot for customers who need to keep inference on their own infrastructure for data residency reasons. We're not chasing parameter count as a marketing number -- we're chasing accuracy per dollar per millisecond on the specific tasks our customers actually run.
[Femi Aduba] You spent years in academic research before Pinewood. What made you leave for industry?
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] I kept publishing papers showing narrow models could match much larger ones on specific tasks, and kept watching the industry chase scale anyway because scale was the exciting story to fund. At some point I decided I'd rather prove the point commercially than keep writing papers that got cited but not acted on.
[Femi Aduba] What's a criticism of your approach that you think is actually fair?
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] That we're slower to support a genuinely novel task than a general-purpose model would be. If a customer needs something our existing narrow models weren't built for, there's real engineering lead time to build and validate a new one, whereas a general model can often attempt it immediately, just less reliably. We accept that trade-off deliberately, but it's a real one, not a hypothetical.
[Femi Aduba] Dr. Lindqvist, thank you for such a candid conversation.
[Dr. Sarah Lindqvist] Thank you, Femi. I enjoy the chance to make the boring, unglamorous case for narrow models out loud.

person_title: Chief Operating Officer of Atlas Reach Logistics
item_title: Rolling out predictive routing across a national fleet
transcript_text:
[Yuki Tanabe] Kwame, Atlas Reach just finished rolling out predictive routing to your entire national fleet. What problem was this actually solving?
[Kwame Asante] Dispatchers were building routes based on yesterday's traffic patterns and today's driver availability, essentially by experience and gut feel, which is genuinely impressive given how complex the problem is, but it doesn't scale past a certain fleet size. We built a system that recalculates optimal routes every fifteen minutes against live traffic, weather, and delivery-window data, and hands dispatchers a recommendation they can accept or override.
[Yuki Tanabe] How did the dispatch team react to a system essentially doing part of their job?
[Kwame Asante] There was real resistance at first, understandably -- some of these dispatchers had fifteen years of experience they felt was being second-guessed by software. What changed minds was framing it as a second opinion they could override, not a replacement, and making the override button genuinely easy to use rather than three menus deep. Adoption climbed a lot once people trusted it wasn't going to quietly punish them for disagreeing with it.
[Yuki Tanabe] What were the actual results once it was fully rolled out?
[Kwame Asante] On-time delivery rate is up around seven percentage points fleet-wide, and average fuel cost per route is down close to twelve percent. The fuel number surprised us more than the on-time number -- we built this primarily for reliability, and the efficiency gain turned out to be almost as large a benefit.
[Yuki Tanabe] Was there a rollout mistake you'd do differently if you were starting over?
[Kwame Asante] We rolled it out to every region simultaneously instead of piloting region by region, and that meant when we found an edge case in how the system handled multi-stop residential routes, it was already live everywhere at once. A staged rollout would have let us catch that in one region before it affected dispatch decisions nationally.
[Yuki Tanabe] How do you think about the driver's side of this, not just dispatch?
[Kwame Asante] Drivers see a proposed route and can flag anything that doesn't match ground truth -- a road closure the system doesn't know about yet, a loading dock that's unexpectedly inaccessible. Those flags feed back into the routing model within the day, so drivers end up training the system almost as much as dispatchers do, even though that wasn't originally how we designed it.
[Yuki Tanabe] What's next on the roadmap for this system?
[Kwame Asante] Extending it to cross-dock scheduling, not just the last-mile routes. Right now the routing system and the warehouse scheduling system don't talk to each other, and there's real efficiency sitting in that gap once a truck's expected arrival time can actually shape which dock door and which loading crew get assigned to it.
[Yuki Tanabe] Kwame, thanks for such a detailed walkthrough.
[Kwame Asante] Thanks, Yuki. Always glad to talk through the operational details most coverage skips over.
